title: Asahi Linux forbids using AI to contribute
content:
Generative AI (LLM) Policy
Generative AI tools using large language models (LLMs) are widespread in software development today. While we acknowledge that these tools do have uses cases, LLMs engender harms to the pillars of Asahi Linux: software freedom, the open-source community, the open Internet, the environment, digital privacy, user consent, and software developers themselves. For more information on the ethical issues of LLM use in open source, we recommend reading SourceHut’s policy
Furthermore, Asahi Linux relies on clean room reverse engineering to ensure our work is legal. We have strict guardrails around binary disassembly and decompilation, and we absolutely forbid the use of leaked materials. While general questions around LLMs and copyright remain unsettled, LLMs pose unique legal risks to reverse engineering projects, as these systems are likely to violate the clean room requirements and taint the resulting code. This risk is amplified with “agentic” approaches, where the human may be unaware of the reverse engineering process. In reverse engineering and science how knowledge is obtained is just as important as the knowledge itself.
Due to these legal and ethical issues, we broadly forbid the use of generative AI tooling for material contributions to Asahi Linux. Enforcement may vary depending on the seriousness of the infraction. A GitHub issue drafted by an LLM may simply be closed with reference to this policy. A contributor using an LLM to interpret a trace made using the m1n1 hypervisor may be issued with a first and final warning. A contributor found to have concealed extensive LLM use will be banned immediately, particularly if they may have accessed unreleased Apple material.

report.summary: Asahi Linux bans generative AI for material contributions, citing clean-room reverse-engineering legal risks and open-source ethical harms.
report.background: Asahi Linux is a community project bringing Linux to Apple Silicon Macs, work that depends heavily on reverse engineering Apple hardware and firmware. Because its legal footing rests on clean-room methods—developers documenting behavior without copying or contaminating code with proprietary or leaked material—the project imposes strict rules around disassembly, decompilation, and source provenance. Generative AI has become common in software development, but LLMs raise unresolved copyright questions and can blur how code or knowledge was obtained. Asahi Linux says LLM use conflicts with its core values: software freedom, community trust, the open Internet, environmental sustainability, digital privacy, user consent, and developers’ interests. The policy follows similar moves in open source, such as SourceHut’s LLM policy, and reflects growing debate over AI-assisted contributions, disclosure, and legal risk in projects that must prove independent development.
key_points: Asahi Linux broadly forbids generative AI tooling for material contributions. Minor cases, such as an LLM-drafted GitHub issue, may simply be closed with a reference to the policy. More serious cases can trigger warnings, and concealed extensive LLM use can lead to an immediate ban, especially if unreleased Apple material may have been accessed.

The central concern is legal contamination. Asahi Linux relies on clean-room reverse engineering, with strict guardrails around disassembly and decompilation and a ban on leaked materials. LLMs may violate clean-room requirements and taint resulting code, and agentic AI can hide how knowledge was obtained. The project insists that how knowledge is obtained matters as much as the knowledge itself.

The policy also cites ethical harms beyond copyright. Asahi Linux says LLMs threaten software freedom, the open-source community, the open Internet, the environment, digital privacy, user consent, and software developers themselves. It points readers to SourceHut’s policy for a fuller argument on LLM use in open source.

Enforcement is graduated by seriousness. An LLM-drafted issue may be closed; using an LLM to interpret a trace from the m1n1 hypervisor may bring a first and final warning; concealing extensive LLM use may bring an immediate ban. This gives maintainers discretion while signaling that provenance and disclosure are central.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Asahi Linux’s policy is a high-profile signal that AI coding tools face provenance and liability scrutiny in legally sensitive open-source work, not just style or quality objections. It may encourage other reverse-engineering and hardware projects to adopt explicit LLM rules, disclosure requirements, and clean-room audits. Developers should assume that AI-assisted issue reports, patches, and trace analysis may be rejected or require disclosure; keeping human-authored evidence and tool logs will matter. Regular users may see slower support for Apple Silicon features if contributors are cautious, but the project argues this protects legal safety, privacy, and community trust. It also adds pressure on AI vendors to provide provenance and compliance features for code generation.
report.tools: Readers can follow Asahi Linux’s policy and SourceHut’s LLM policy as models for AI contribution rules. For technical context, watch m1n1, Asahi Linux’s open-source hypervisor and debugging tool used for Apple Silicon reverse engineering; it illustrates why trace interpretation and provenance are sensitive. Also watch Asahi Linux’s kernel patches and clean-room documentation workflows. There is no AI tool to try here; the relevant tool is policy and provenance tracking.
